title: Developer Turns MacBook Trackpad Into a Speaker Using Haptic Motor
excerpt: A new free tool makes a MacBook's Force Touch trackpad produce speech and music by vibrating its glass, even when the computer's speakers are...
content_html:
A new free tool makes a MacBook's Force Touch trackpad produce speech and music by vibrating its glass, even when the computer's speakers are muted.


The open-source project is called "NO SPEAKER," and comes from developer Cody Collier, who recently shared shared a demonstration on X. The tool uses the small haptic motor that normally makes a Force Touch trackpad feel as though it clicks. Driving that motor at different frequencies makes the glass vibrate fast enough to produce audible sounds.

The demo lasts around a minute and a half and includes speech, a melody, a beat, and a short rap. Users can also slide a finger across the trackpad to change the pitch of a tone, enter their own text for it to speak, or choose another installed macOS voice. The tool does not turn the trackpad into a normal audio output for playing music files or sound from other apps.

i made my macbook trackpad talk using only the vibrations from its haptic motor

my speakers are muted, every sound you hear is coming from the trackpad itself

open source, try it here: github.com/os6/nospeaker

— cody (@codycollier) November 22, 2026

To generate speech, the software starts with a voice created by macOS's built-in text-to-speech feature. It breaks the recording into tiny sections and picks out the main sound frequencies that make the words recognizable. The motor then reproduces a simplified version of those sounds through the trackpad.

The result is a quiet, robotic voice. Collier says the words are easier to follow when reading the text displayed alongside them, and recommends placing the MacBook on a table to make the sound easier to hear.

The tool uses parts of macOS that Apple does not make available for third-party developers to use, namely the "MultitouchSupport" framework. These let it control how fast and strongly the trackpad vibrates, rather than simply trigger a preset click. Since Apple does not officially support this use-case, a future macOS update could stop the tool from working.

Collier says the tool keeps the haptic motor within its normal maximum strength, but it is unknown whether prolonged use could affect the trackpad's lifespan. NO SPEAKER requires a Force Touch trackpad and macOS Monterey or later on Apple silicon, or macOS Ventura or later on Intel. The tool is free and available now on GitHub.
